title: Lesson Objectives Are Overrated
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane challenges the common observation-tool assumption that every moment of a lesson should visibly connect to one stated objective. He describes his own teaching moving toward lessons with several small, separately-purposed chunks rather than one unifying goal, listing seven categories of classroom activity that don't tie neatly to 'today's math concept': retrieval practice, momentum-building routines at the start of class, formative assessment (which he finds more useful the following lesson than as a same-day exit ticket), covering for individual student follow-up, method-selection practice using Craig Barton's 'SSDD' (same surface, different deep) problems, prerequisite-skill checks, and previewing future topics. His underlying argument is that forcing every lesson element into service of one objective produces artificial coherence at the cost of genuinely useful but disconnected instructional moves -- retrieval practice, in particular, is valuable precisely because it revisits old material unconnected to today's new content.
points: Kane's central move is separating 'the lesson has one objective' from 'each chunk of the lesson has a clear goal' -- he keeps the second while rejecting the first as an artificial constraint.

His critique of same-day exit tickets (they produce 'a lot of false positives') and preference for next-lesson formative checks is a specific, testable claim about when formative assessment is actually informative.
Citing Craig Barton's SSDD ('same surface, different deep') problems as his method-selection tool shows a direct cross-pollination between the Eedi/Barton ecosystem and Kane's own classroom practice.

His seven-category list (retrieval, momentum, formative assessment, individual follow-up, method selection, prerequisites, previewing) gives teachers a concrete menu of legitimate non-objective-aligned lesson components, not just a critique of the old model.
quotes: To some people there's this Platonic ideal of a lesson where the entire class from the moment students walk in builds toward the objective.
All of that comes from this assumption that each lesson should have exactly one goal, and everything that happens should be in service of that goal.
Retrieval practice is best in short chunks with a variety of problems. It doesn't fit nicely into a lesson goal but it's an important ingredient in teaching.
I don't find exit tickets very helpful. After spending a lesson working on a skill there will be a lot of false positives.
A strategy I love is what Craig Barton calls SSDD, or same surface different deep, problems.
One unintended consequence of the idea that every lesson should be laser-focused on a clear, specific goal is a lack of mixed practice.
